CITY_PDB holds, per city, the carrier-neutral facilities and network
presences from PeeringDB (within 50 km or same city name) and the ASN
count of its country from bgp.he.net, pulled 2026-10-25.

- Transit: the regional multiplier is scaled by competition, up to 1.8x

  and hand-set markets (Korea, Belgian red tape) keep their price.

- Offers: countries with 2000+ ASNs bring extra ISP customers.
Calibration: drop a redundant guard and a one-caller helper

Custom routing metric for links

A link's routing metric could only be one of four presets (Prefer,
Normal, Avoid, Backup only). Links now also get a Custom option, closer
to how real networks tune IGP metrics:

- Multiplier mode scales the distance cost, (km + 60) × 0.1 to 100.
- Cost mode sets an exact cost, 1 to 65535 like an OSPF metric.

The preset buttons stay plain. Picking Custom explains how a link's cost
is worked out and lists what each preset comes to on that link. Choosing
Custom starts from the current preset and switching modes keeps the
effective cost, so nothing moves until the player changes the value.
Like the presets, it applies to every link between the two cities.

The cost formula lives in one helper, linkW(), used by compute() and the
traceroute paths. Custom links store mk/mv, which sanitize() repairs and
clamps; old saves load unchanged. The link panel skips its daily
re-render while the number field has focus, and Enter applies the value.

Tests cover routing equivalence with the presets, rerouting by cost,
mode switching, input clamping, saves, and the panel at desktop and
phone width. French, Italian and Portuguese for the new strings.
Perf on the big network: no change beyond noise, routing identical to
main.

Rework DDoS generation, mitigation accounting and NOC reporting

Scale normal attacks with network demand, level and gaming exposure, with
randomized sizes, durations, overlapping attacks and distributed ingress.
Set average sizes to three times the non-gaming baseline at one gaming
customer and eight times at fifty. Keep Flood Season escalating after its
challenge ends.

Add gaming-specific vectors, Memcached amplification and ACK floods.
Account for upstream scrubbing, Flowspec and shared scrubbing capacity in
sequence. Show precise mitigation totals and one destination-based
scrubbing detour in existing live attack cards.

Keep each source-to-scrubbing route distinct in link traffic breakdowns,
including the source label, Open button and map highlight.

Include deterministic tests, old-save migration and translations.
rewrite changelog
Merge latest main into codex/ddos-scaling-and-mitigation
Merge origin/main into codex/ddos-scaling-and-mitigation
Add editable optic counts to fiber link panels

Add bulk PNI ordering across networks and POPs

Add two actions to the NOC Traffic tab:
- Order PNIs with one network at every shared POP.
- Order PNIs with all eligible networks at every shared POP, including
  long-tail peers.

Both actions offer a selectable port size and preview new connections,
upgrades, total setup costs, additional monthly charges and blocked sites.
Upgrade smaller PNIs while preserving larger connections, pending orders
and existing LAG members. Reserve router capacity across the batch and
account for pending speed and LAG augments to avoid overbooking ports.

Require the full setup budget before placing any orders. Reuse normal
peering policies, minimum port sizes and provisioning delays, then
recompute and save once for the entire batch. Keep large global previews
compact with collapsible network and blocked-connection lists.

Translate the new UI into all five supported languages and add tests for
single-network and global ordering, capacity, budgets, repeated clicks,
save migration, and mobile keyboard interaction.

Validation:
- Build and translation checks pass.
- 308 of 309 tests pass. The existing subsea reach test also fails on
  origin/main because the Windows locale uses a dot as the thousands
  separator where the assertion expects a comma.
- Chromium desktop and phone checks pass with the supplied save.
- Big-network benchmark against origin/main: dashboard tabs take
  16.8 -> 17.6 ms on desktop and 77.1 -> 80.7 ms on a simulated phone
  (median of 15 runs). Routing results are identical, with no slowdowns
  beyond the benchmark's noise threshold.

Add real-time sales automation and automatic paid repairs

Add independent toggles for auto-accept in Deals and auto-pay repairs in
NOC. Save both settings and default them off for older or malformed saves.

Check sales every five wall-clock seconds regardless of game speed, and
show a small countdown on Accept buttons in Deals, city offers and fiber
broker offers. Only sign when all requirements, locations, equipment and
service capacity are ready. Trial the added demand before accepting it,
protect healthy existing customers and account for booked future events.

Use the existing paid repair action for affordable active incidents,
including slow router reboots. Skip expired incidents, removed equipment,
DDoS attacks and repairs that were already rushed. Pause both automations
with the game, hidden pages and open dialogs.

Translate the controls into all five supported languages and cover timing,
countdowns, capacity, budgets, repair payments, persistence, mobile controls
and trial rollback with deterministic tests. Chromium checks verify about
five real seconds at both 0.5x and 8x game speed and exercise the supplied
large save without changing the save file.

Show auto-accept countdowns only for ready offers

Hide the countdown when an offer has unmet requirements, missing locations,
expired terms or insufficient service capacity. Keep manual acceptance
available with its existing behavior.

Share capacity previews across the Deals, city and fiber views, reuse them
between automatic checks, and invalidate them after actions or incidents.
Check changing requirements immediately and always perform a fresh full
validation before automatically signing a contract.

Add regression tests for blocked offers, requirements becoming fulfilled
or unfulfilled, capacity changes and preview reuse. All 17 automation tests
pass; the full independent branch passes 314 of 315 tests, with only the
pre-existing locale-dependent subsea formatting failure remaining.

serves them all. Same groups, same order, same result (routing-reference and speed tests).

commit.message:
Billing: a recompute after the day tick no longer counts today's 95th-percentile sample twice

dayTick() routes the day, then appends today's transit use to t.hist. Every
compute() after that (any click, the intern, the sales trial) took the last 29
entries of t.hist, which now end on today, and added today's use again: today
counted twice and the 30th day back dropped out. So compute() gave a different
transit bill the second time after each day. p95() now leaves today's sample out
once S.hist says the day has been recorded.

This was the only part of compute() that was not a pure function of S. The rest
of the drift round 1 saw (R right after dayTick vs. a fresh compute) is dayTick
itself changing S after its compute (customers churning, events ending), which
is intended: the next day routes the new state. Scenic circuits' hysteresis is
documented, with a test that two calls converge.

commit.message:
Attacks arrive as on 1.36 again: drop the distributed multi-ingress flood model

Frederic's call for 2.0: keep #153's fixes, NOC breakdown, new vectors, gaming risk
and overlapping attacks, but not the per-port model. It split every flood over each
ingress port with traffic (over a thousand on a big network), stored them all in the
save, routed one pinned flow per port, and with it came the build-order and
victim-scoring bugs found in review.

Each attack is again one entry port at the victim (a.entry): upstream clean-pipe,
Flowspec on the victim's router, IX blackholing, a sacrificial PNI and RouteScript
filter it in that order (ddosMitigation), then scrubbing; what leaks is junk at the
victim spread like its traffic, exactly as on main. Saves from 2.0 builds with
a.entries load: sanitize drops the shares and a 'distributed' entry becomes 'edge'.
Removed: R.ingressPorts, ddosEntries/ddosFold/ddosSlices/ddosCities/ddosHasIx, pinned
flows (and the pinned-rank handling in routing and its reference), the mixed-TCAM
line and the 'across N ports' message, and their tests; the scrubbing source-city
test now uses two victims sharing one center. CHANGELOG #153 bullets describe what
ships and credit #153.

commit.message:
Submarine upgrades that change nothing on a cable can't be bought (#198)

Premium submarine terminals and Optical engineering only extend the
long-haul modes of the coherent optics. On many cable lengths (all of
the Atlantic, and about 17,000-18,500 km like Atlanta to Sydney) neither
changes what any optic carries, yet both could be bought.

subHelps() compares every optic's rate with and without the upgrade,
counting an upgrade that only helps together with the other one. The
link panel disables Install with a note, ACT.subUpgrade refuses, and
the cable order screen disables the toggle and only quotes and charges
picks that still help on the chosen design.

Map: a link's curve only measures the cities that could be in its way

measures as clear; leaving it out gives the same curve. About 4x faster, and
the curves on the big fixture are byte-identical.

commit.message:
A carrier's own transit port takes its traffic, with a Carry here switch for other POPs

Transit ports at a POP shared load by free capacity whatever the traffic
was for, so Level Tree's own traffic went out of a Tell-Ya port about
half the time. Traffic bound for a carrier, or for a network that buys
transit from it, now goes out of that carrier's port at the same POP
first (the shorter AS path). Each such port is still an ordinary transit
exit, so POPs without one use it when nothing nearer has room.

A new switch on each transit port, Carry here, pulls that traffic from
every POP across your network to this port. The default, Nearest port,
keeps using the closest transit port from POPs that have no port of the
carrier. The switch only shows when another carrier's port could take
the traffic instead.

Prefer-marked ports, Backup only, RouteScript and Auto-TE keep their say,
and any Prefer-marked transit port switches the rule off. Traceroute
follows the same rule and says why it picked an exit. The setting is
repaired in sanitize(); old saves load with it off.

The routing reference test now has several carriers sharing POPs, ports
that carry, backup ports and RouteScript, and its reference loop knows
the new ranks.

commit.message:
Routing keeps its structural tables between calls and runs its hot loops as small functions, identical results

compute() was one 33 KB function that V8 never kept optimised: it ran in baseline code, boxing every number,
and was recompiled in the background (about a second of compile each time on a loaded machine) only to deopt.
Its stages now run as closures of their own (compute's own bytecode: 7.7 KB) and the money is computeMoney().
The shortest paths and the exit lists (okBy, reach, BRJ/LIST, DSEL) are kept between calls under keys built
from everything they depend on (29-route-cache.js). Exits and paths have one object shape each.
The equivalence tests compare cached against uncached routing; tests/route-cache.test.js checks the keys.

commit.message:
Routing adds up per-kind traffic in typed arrays and keeps its group array's storage: half the allocation per compute

R.egT and R.netEg were summed by key in push(), which boxes every new value; they are now Float64Array sums written
back after routing, in the same order and key order. The first group G was emptied with length=0 for every flow,
which gives back its storage so the next push allocates it again; it is now G[0..GN). 27.5 MB -> 13.5 MB per compute.
